source.title: Binary Sparse Coding for Interpretability
source.authors: Lucia Quirke; Stepan Shabalin; Nora Belrose

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates explanations and interpretability scores for sparse-coder features, not neuron poles. Its results refine the claim that such scores reliably establish a feature's job: it reports a counterexample to a perfect-scoring explanation and frequency-sensitive interpretability results.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure the share of neuron poles with one or more jobs, test InceptionV1 neurons, or build neuron-based attribution graphs. Its own relevant measurements concern sparse-coder features in SmolLM2. The cited work and its results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures explanation scores for sparse-coder (SAE and transcoder) features in SmolLM2, not for the model's own neurons. None of its results bear on any version, since every version concerns neurons. Its only statement about neurons is the cited view that most neurons are polysemantic [2, 12], which is background and not a result. The feature-level findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that binarisation improves unweighted feature interpretability but raises reconstruction error and patched loss, and creates uninterpretable ultra-high-frequency features. In SmolLM2-135M, frequency-adjusted scores slightly favour continuous coders, although the single-seed 1.7B run favours binary on every metric. They also report that finetuned binary coders do better at sparse probing. They conclude polysemanticity may be ineliminable and do not recommend binary coders for most purposes. They also note that auto-interp scores can overestimate interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains binary and continuous sparse autoencoders and transcoders, then scores generated explanations of their features. It does not audit neuron poles or apply the original neuron-level method.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability comparisons depend on whether scores are unweighted or adjusted for feature firing frequency.

fits_no_version.finding: A non-cherrypicked binary skip-transcoder feature with perfect fuzzing and detection scores has non-activating instances of 'search' words. The authors say the scores 'can over-estimate the true interpretability of features', partly because negatives were random rather than adversarial.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Auto-interpretability scores with random negatives overstate how well an explanation predicts where a sparse-coder feature fires.

fits_no_version.finding: Binarisation raises unweighted feature interpretability but creates ultra-high-frequency uninterpretable features (Fig. 6, 7). In SmolLM2-135M, frequency-weighted scores favour continuous coders (Fig. 3); in the single-seed 1.7B run, binary is higher on all four metrics (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing activation-strength variation from sparse coders shifts polysemanticity into high-frequency features rather than eliminating it.

record.problems: The study focuses on one training corpus and reports that some sparse coders have many dead features. The SmolLM2-1.7B comparison is a single-seed run. The feature explanation case study is one example, and the authors note that the evaluation used random rather than adversarially selected negative examples. These are sparse-coder feature results, not neuron-pole results.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the rows to V6 and V7 while itself noting that the units are sparse-coder features, not neurons. The versions specify neurons, so the links are removed and no verdicts are given. The neuron-polysemanticity statement in the introduction is only cited. Rows R2 to R7 are comparisons of the study's own method against a baseline. Figure 8 (interpretability vs ablation effect) and Figure 7 (firing rates) are not captured as rows, but they too concern features only.

rows.subject: SmolLM2-135M
rows.operation_detail: Inspected activating and non-activating examples for a binary skip-transcoder feature with perfect auto-interpretability fuzzing and detection scores.

conditions.value: non-cherrypicked feature selected from those with perfect auto-interpretability scores

rows.measure: Whether the explanation predicted feature activation on examples
rows.baseline: The generated explanation received perfect auto-interpretability fuzzing and detection scores
rows.value: The authors found instances of search-related words that did not activate the feature, so the perfect scores overstated its interpretability.
rows.note: The authors attribute the overestimate partly to using random rather than adversarially selected non-activating examples. This is a sparse-coder feature, not a neuron.
rows.check: The unit is a binary skip-transcoder feature, not a neuron, so it does not bear on V6. At feature level the overestimate is shown: non-activating 'search' instances exist despite perfect scores. The record's state of 'partial' understates this.

rows.subject: SmolLM2-135M
rows.operation_detail: Compared binary and continuous skip-transcoder feature explanations using unweighted fuzzing F1 across layers and k values.
rows.value: Binary coders matched or outperformed continuous coders across all shown layers and k values; figure values
rows.uncertainty: Three seeds; error bars are ±1 standard error of the mean
rows.note: The plotted comparison does not report the fraction of features attaining a defined good-score threshold. These are feature explanations, not neuron explanations.
rows.check: This row compares sparse-coder feature scores between the study's own binary method and the continuous baseline. It is not neuron explanation scoring, so it does not bear on V7.

rows.subject: SmolLM2-135M
rows.operation_detail: Compared binary and continuous skip-transcoder feature explanations using frequency-weighted fuzzing F1 across layers and k values.
rows.value: Binary coders were often less interpretable by this metric; figure values
rows.uncertainty: Three seeds; error bars are ±1 standard error of the mean
rows.note: The paper states that frequency-adjusted scores for continuous sparse coders were slightly better overall. The metric is for sparse-coder features, not neurons.
rows.check: This is a method comparison (binary vs continuous) on sparse-coder features, not neurons. 'Partial' has no meaning against V7 here.

rows.subject: SmolLM2-1.7B

rows.note: A mean score does not establish what proportion of features achieved a good score. The evaluated units are sparse-coder features.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method with a baseline on sparse-coder features in SmolLM2-1.7B, single seed. It does not bear on neurons.
